weaknesses: The evaluation is not competitive for a top-tier AI venue. There are no direct baselines against SMILES/SELFIES LLMs, graph-based optimization methods, fragment-based optimization, oracle-guided methods such as DrugAssist, or simple building-block/random-neighbor heuristics.

The proposed architecture is plausible: GNN-encoded molecular blocks are integrated into a decoder-only LLM, and the paper gives useful high-level details on data construction, training, and tokenizer design.

The evaluation includes multiple molecule-generation baselines, validity and synthetic-accessibility metrics, an Allchemy retrosynthesis check on sampled outputs, and out-of-vocabulary FDA-drug experiments.
The appendices provide substantial dataset statistics and additional implementation detail, which helps clarify the intended training setup.
weaknesses: The central empirical evidence relies heavily on learned oracle models for ADMET properties, and similar oracle-generated labels appear in the training data. This creates a serious risk of oracle overfitting or leakage, so the reported property improvements do not convincingly establish real functional improvement.

The synthesizability claims are overstated. Building-block compatibility and SA or retrosynthesis scores do not guarantee practical makeability under automated synthesis, especially without experimental synthesis, reaction yields, route details, protection/deprotection feasibility, or block availability constraints.

The baseline comparison is not sufficiently controlled. The paper lacks strong baselines operating in the same constrained building-block search space, and prompting, decoding, invalid-output handling, and optimization budgets for LLM baselines are not described in enough detail.

There are few ablations isolating the contributions of the modular tokenizer, GNN block encoder, natural-language supervision, synthesis constraints, data mixture, vocabulary size, or iterative reasoning procedure. As a result, it is unclear which part of mCLM drives the gains.

The reported metrics are mostly averages without confidence intervals, paired significance tests, per-molecule distributions, novelty/diversity analysis, similarity-to-parent constraints, or failure-case analysis. Several properties appear saturated or hard to interpret, making the claimed average improvements less convincing.

Reproducibility is limited: code, data, tokenizer rules, model weights, exact vocabularies, splits, prompts, and generated molecules are only promised upon publication, and important details of the evaluation pipeline remain underspecified.

The paper makes broad claims about functional and makeable molecule generation, rescuing failed clinical candidates, and enabling non-specialist molecule design, but the evidence is mostly in silico and not strong enough to support these conclusions for a top-tier AI venue.
